items.title: improve the string match itself.
items.creator: andy
items.box:
WHAT IS: probabilityStringMatch(A, B)
- A exactly equal to B: 1.0. Not a string, or one side empty: 0.
- Otherwise the shorter string is graded against the longer, both lowercased and accents folded, as the weighted mean of four signals:
  - match (1.0): whole 1.0, starts with 0.7, found inside 0.35, only some of its words 0.15; no word found at all: 0.
  - coverage (0.2): the shorter's length over the longer's.
  - words (0.3): the share of the shorter's characters found in the longer's words, whole words first, then the best part of a word.
  - order (0.25): the longest run of matched words in the same order.
- Upper and lower case cost nothing: relay against Relay scores 1.0.
- Distance costs nothing: matched words side by side and 498 words apart score alike on every signal but match.

HOW WE MAKE IT BETTER
1. Case counts: 0.000001 is subtracted for every character whose case differs, counted over the characters that matched ignoring case. Relay ranks above relay and reLay for Relay; it orders ties and moves nothing else.
2. Distance counts, and more than order: a fifth signal, proximity = matched words / words spanned from the first match to the last (side by side 1.0). People type words in any order, but words far apart usually belong to different thoughts, so proximity weighs 0.35 and order drops from 0.25 to 0.15. That ratio is a guess.
3. The weights are set by hand for now, and are meant to be learned later from what makes a user happier.

chat.text: what is there right now?

Today: both strings lowercased and accents folded, so case costs nothing (Relay vs relay = 1.0); then 4 weighted signals: exact/starts-with/contains/some-words (1.0), length coverage (0.2), word match (0.3), word order (0.25).
Order counts, distance does not: relay key with 498 words between scores 0.40, side by side at the start 0.71.
Starts-with outweighs length: relay key at the start of 500 words (0.71) beats the relay key answers (0.56).
But "Relay" matches "Relay" better than "relay" matches "Relay", true or false? subtract 0.001 from probability for every character that is a case-missmatch.

True as you mean it, false today: Relay vs Relay and relay vs Relay both score 1.0.
With 0.001 per case-mismatched character, relay vs Relay becomes 0.999, and any other match drops the same way, never below 0.

Se the coal is sequencing the better matches ahead of worse matches, so if we just subtract 0.000001 per mismatched character-case, after 1000 characters with wrong case we still only used 0.001 of the 1.0 budget, but sequencing is achieved.

Agreed: 0.000001 per case-mismatched character only breaks ties, so Relay ranks above relay for Relay and nothing else moves.
The count is over the characters that matched ignoring case (the exact, prefix or found part, and matched words); unmatched characters have no case to compare.
absolutely. any human will tell you that Relay is not exactly the same as relay, or reLay
even visually
Recorded in the box: your Relay question line now reads as the rule, 0.000001 per case-mismatched character; the rest of your draft is untouched.
Yes: the case penalty orders what the eye sees as closer first.
and distance between matching tokens is definitely an indicator of a worse match.

Agreed, and today nothing measures it. Proposal: a proximity signal = matched words / words spanned from the first match to the last, so side by side is 1.0 and relay ... 498 words ... key is 2/500.
Should it weigh like word order (0.25), a real signal rather than a tie-breaker?
it should have mabe the same weight as word order... hard to say: i didn't think it through yet. this is where i'd have a machine learn what makes a user happier......
Recorded in the box: proximity weighted like word order (0.25) for now, the weights to be learned later from what makes a user happier.

agreed.

can you replace the text in the box with a concise summary of what is, and how we make it better?
The box now holds the summary: what the match does today, then the three changes (case, distance, weights learned later).
honest answer please. is distance more important than sequence? your guess? (i have a guess now)

My guess: distance matters more. People type words in any order (key relay for relay key), but two words 500 apart usually belong to different thoughts.
In short labels both barely matter; in long text distance separates a hit from a coincidence.
agreed. pub in box like that with a guessed weight ratio for now, and saying it is a guess.
In the box: proximity 0.35, order down to 0.15, marked as a guess.
green?

items.title: shell element list-search-container.
items.creator: andy
items.box:
A shell element: a list with its search, looking the same everywhere it is used.

LAYOUT
[set of filters: icons, or word + icon, checked]
[search string input, its clear button inside it on the right] [search button]
[count line]
[list]

CONFIGURATION (what each use sets): one plain object given at creation, callbacks in it, no registry. The shape:

shellCreateListSearch(container, {
  server: 'deskVerify',                 // the server searched (its stream too)
  verb: 'fallout.reds',                 // the search verb invoked
  args: function (text, filters) {},    // the verb's arguments from the words and the filter values
  filters: [{                           // declared, drawn by the container, the same everywhere
    name: 'outcome',
    choices: [{ value: 'red', icon: '❌', word: 'fail' }, { value: 'green', icon: '✅', word: 'success' }, { value: '', word: 'both' }],
    test: function (row, value) {}      // a probability, 0 to 1: 0 leaves the row out, 1 keeps it as it is, between lowers it; never raises it
  }],
  paint: function (row) {},             // one row's html
  press: function (row) {},             // a press on a row (Fallout: its history dialog)
  empty: 'No test matches.'             // the empty-list sentence
})

A row is the object an answer item's label carries; paint, press and test all take that same object. The words are matched against the whole row (probabilityStringObjectMatch), so nothing configures which text is searched.

WHERE IT LIVES
shell/shared/js/listSearch.js, loaded by an app on demand, as deskElement.js is.

WHAT EVERY SEARCH IT CALLS ANSWERS
{items: [{key, label}], more, total}: key is the identity of what the row shows (one per test, per peer, per item), label the row as json, more true when the answer was capped, total how many matched in all. deskVerify is brought to this in G29.5.

BEHAVIOUR (the same for every use)
- The bucket knows nothing of string matching; the container scores every cached row with probabilityStringObjectMatch per keystroke multiplied by every filter's test, and hands the numbers to bucket.sort. A filter only lowers: the words decide the order among the rows the filters let through.
- Rows are keyed by the key the search answer carries; that key is the identity of what the row shows, so a row a later search brings again replaces the older one.
- Every row any search brought is kept in a cache, a probabilityBucket, unbounded.
- Each character typed or erased redraws the list from the cache at once, ranked by probabilityStringMatch: best matches on top, every row the filters let through shown.
- The server calls MUST be serialized: at most one request of the element on the wire at a time, every verb it calls included. No typing pause: each character typed or erased asks the server at once when nothing is on the wire; while a request is out, the latest words go the moment its answer returns. The round trip paces the server, the cache paces the screen.
- The count line says how many match, and that the answer was partial when the server capped it.

items.box:
Fallout talks to deskVerify only. Its Reds list is built with shellCreateListSearch (G29.4), and its own search machinery is deleted.

DESKVERIFY
- Its search keys each test row by the test's identity, its file and its key, not its database record; it answers more and total.

The peer picker, contactSelector, becomes a thin wrapper around shellCreateListSearch (G29.4), for Contacts, chatter and every place a peer is picked.

COLUMNS

FILTERS
- One filter per state, owned (★), blocked and held, each shown only when the list holds any contact in that state; each narrows the list to that state.

WHAT THE ROWS CARRY
- contact.search, a node verb, changes by Andy's grant of the changed verb: it answers each peer as {key: its public key, label: json {name, owned, blocked, held}}, so the star is drawn from the row.

EVERY LIST BEHAVES THE SAME

BEHAVIOUR BEYOND THE SHARED LIST
- The app repaints one row when a peer's presence or status changes, without asking the server.

- This item is Contacts: the peer picker and hub's contact.search, ranked with the probability modules instead of the old search.

Grants on the shared list: one line of selectors that filter, a search within them, a table of grants below, the same look as every other search.

THE LINE
- One line at the top, nothing stacked: [whose access] [choose a server] [choose a verb] [Grant].
- The three selectors are dropdowns of the shared list, as the contact selector already is; the server and verb selectors leave their native selects.
- The verb selector shows only once a server is chosen; it offers that server's verbs.
- The selectors are filters: each one chosen narrows the list to its choice; one left unchosen means all (every peer, every server, every verb).
- Grant grants what the line names: the chosen peer the chosen server, one verb when a verb is chosen, all its verbs when none is. It needs a peer and a server: until a contact is chosen the line shows Select a contact in its place, and until a server is chosen Select a server; no blanket grant to every peer.
- A server that names a bundle (its DEPENDENCIES) offers Grant the bundle on the same line once it is chosen.

THE SEARCH AND THE TABLE
- The search bar below the line searches within the line's filters, ranked as every search is, with the rank bar and the marks.
- Below it the grants in a small table: the peer's name, the path, deprecated when no server serves the path today, and each row's own Revoke.
- The page holds the grants (jobs.authSearch with no words, bounded as every answer) and ranks them itself, as Files does.
- jobs.authSearch moves to the new search as well, as every search does one by one: words ranked by the probability modules, best first, each grant answered as a json label {name, key, path}; its old search goes.

items.box:
Full file-stat streaming and a file-level search in Files, end to end. No contents yet: the next item (G29.7) adds them.

THE STREAM
- The node streams the tree to the page as it does, the watcher's updates, now each with its stat: size and modified, for every create and change; a delete carries none.
- The first load is a stream of the root folder's entries, the run folder the first and only record shown at the start; no list-size limit applies there.
- The shell holds it (shell.js currentFiles): every path, its kind and its stat.

FILES ON THE SHARED LIST
- A new shell element, fileSelector (shell/js/fileSelector.js), built as contactSelector is: a wrapper on shellCreateListSearch over the shell's mirror, with a pane face and a dropdown face; the Files app is a container for its pane, and any app picking a file uses its dropdown.
- The shell holds the rows, its mirror keyed by path; each list keeps its own bucket and bucket state over them, since two open lists rank by different words.
- Names and paths are searched in the page and never reach the server.
- fileSelector replaces pathSelector, the older picker over the same mirror, which is deleted.
- The text editor picks its file with the fileSelector dropdown in place of its path field.
- Every display has the stat columns: size and modified, right-justified, and the mimetype icon before the name.
- No words: the tree appearance, rows in path order, one square indent per slash, a folder row folding the rows under it.
- Words typed: list mode, the rows ranked best first, each with its full path, the matched parts marked, as every search.

TWO MODES IN THE SHARED LIST
- Pane and dropdown come from G29.9, the item before this one.
- The dropdown's field stands inline like any input control; only the pane pops up under it.

THE CORE'S FOLDER LISTINGS
- No new verb: an empty search is the whole tree, and the one shared helper is the shell's tree read with no words.
- Desk's plugin finder keeps the rows plugins/<name>/<name>.js; an app's own folder (kernel's scanDirectory) keeps the rows under its folder; server-side loaders read their own folders as they do.

THE NODE'S fs.search
- It stays, on the node's own cached tree (the watcher's), as Files sits on the shell's: the agents' file tool and every caller that is not a page.
- It ranks words by the same probability modules as the shared list, best first; fs.search's patterns (* and ?) and gradedSearch with them go.
- G29.7 adds the contents to it.

AFTER THE FIRST BUILD
- No words: every folder starts folded; a press on a folder unfolds or folds it, in the pane and in the dropdown alike, and is never a pick.
- Words typed: every match shows, nothing folded.
- In the tree the icon stands right before the name, after the indent.
- An open dropdown keeps its current row in view as the keys move it, and its field shows that current row.
- A file dropdown takes a hidden type filter the app configures (extensions or mimetype prefixes); folders always show. The text editor passes its text types.
- A folder-picker mode is out of scope here.
- An open dropdown takes the width its rows need, up to the page width: inside a popup the rows' table takes its own width, and a file name is never cut short.
- Home and End belong to the list, as up and down do, from the search box too: they move the current row to the top and the bottom. Pane and dropdown alike; the search box's cursor moves with the mouse or left and right.
- The file list has one filter, words in: names | paths. Names, the default, matches the words against the file name only; paths against the whole path, folders included.
- A folded folder carries no mark after its name: an ellipsis there reads as a name cut short.

items.box:
Nothing in it is specific to contacts: it makes the search list's pane and its dropdown one system, and puts the features common to lists into the shared element, for one look and feel.

WHAT EXISTS (shellCreateListSearch, shell/shared/js/listSearch.js, today)
- Rows 1 to 3 in one pane: the filter row (filters declared, each shown only when its when(rows) says so), the search row (box, its clear button inside on the right, the search button), a count line, the list.
- One keyed cache, an unbounded probabilityBucket; each keystroke ranks it in the page (probabilityStringObjectMatch times every filter's test), all rows shown, the best on top.
- The server asked through api, server, verb and args: serialized, one request on the wire, no typing pause; the slot lent to the app (list.ask); a publish on its stream asks again.
- paint(row), press(row), empty; refresh() and redraw().
- contactSelector holds a dropdown of its own (a button opening the list) and marks its chosen row with a bold name.

WHAT IS NEW
- Two modes, pane and dropdown, never both in one place: a list is the one or the other (chatter is a pane). The dropdown is just a pop-up pane: closed, a field showing the chosen row's name, or a placeholder; opened by a click on it, the whole pane pops up under it, rows 1 to 3 exactly as the pane looks, and shuts on a pick, escape or a click outside.
- In a pane the keys are available wherever the focus is in it, the search box or the list; in an open dropdown alike.
- Two tiers, set in the create function: rows the page already holds (a function answering them: the shell's file mirror, a monitor's stream, a caller's own contacts), ranked in the page and never asking the server; and the optional server hook as today, its rows joining the same cache. Most lists use both; Files and the monitors, the page alone.
- A press on a row: in dropdown mode a pick; in pane mode the optional details(row) hook, which opens the row's dialog (a file's contents, a contact's details); with no hook, a pick there too.
- Keys: up and down move the current row, home and end go to the top or bottom, enter presses it, escape closes an open dropdown; while the search box has the focus home and end stay the text cursor's.
- The current row drawn by the list itself, the same everywhere: a slightly brighter background across the whole row.
- The matched parts marked: the list hands paint a mark(text) that wraps each matched word, so every search gets it.
- contactSelector drops its own dropdown and its bold name and passes the mode; chatter's new-chat picker and grants follow with no change of their own.

items.title: Contents filter: words searched inside text files
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Search inside files: words found in the contents of text files, the files ranked by how well their contents match.

THE FILTER
- The file list has one filter with three mutually exclusive choices, words in: names | paths | contents. Names is the default. Contents alone is find-in-files; the three scores mean different things and are never mixed.
- The page asks the node only in contents; names and paths stay searched in the page.

THE CONTENTS SCORE
- The search words are one cluster: each line of a text file is scored against the whole expression by probabilityStringMatch, and a line that holds any of the words is a matched line.
- A file's contents score is the average quality of its matched lines x m / (m + 10), m the number of matched lines, never the file's length: 1 line 0.09, 10 lines 0.5, 40 lines 0.8.

THE VERB (approved by Andy)
- fs.search takes contents: yes beside q. With it the node reads text files up to 1 MB (text/*, json, javascript; larger ones are never read) and ranks the files by their contents score alone, each answered with label {path, score, line}: the score and the first matched line. Without it fs.search answers as before.

THE LIST
- No found line in the rows: the list ranks the files.
- Every search on the shared list shows its ranking: in search mode the left-most column is a 3em weight bar, right adjusted (it grows leftward from the column's right edge), full for the best row and proportionally shorter for the others; with no words the column is gone.
- A press on a file found by its contents opens the viewer with the words marked and its first match in view.
- In the text editor: a file picked in its own file picker in contents opens marked with the picker's words. Opened any other way the editor shows no marks.
- Every change of the words snaps the list to its top: the best row becomes the current row and the list scrolls to the top, in every list, pane and dropdown, until the user moves the current row.

Suggestion, two parts, both counted over the whole file, case ignored, partial words included:
- coverage: the share of the words that occur at all (screw driver, only screw found: 0.5).
- frequency: hits counted and saturating, f = hits / (hits + 3): 1 hit 0.25, 3 hits 0.5, 10 hits 0.77, 100 hits 0.97.
- contents score = coverage x (0.5 + 0.5 x f), so a file holding every word once (0.625) still beats one holding half the words a hundred times (0.49).

One refinement on the fixed number: m / 10000 keeps the contents score tiny (40 lines: 0.004), so averaged with a name score it would vanish. m / (m + K) does the same against a fixed K but stays between 0 and 1: with K = 10, 1 line 0.09, 10 lines 0.5, 40 lines 0.8, 1000 lines 0.99.

items.title: Progress protocol: one published message, one bar
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
One progress protocol for every appServer and for the transient processes that remain in SpiritOS, so every app (Jobs, Desk, any that sends off jobs) draws the same progress bar.
The Jobs list (goal/G29.14) gets its progress column from this item.

THE JOB CYCLE
- A job is: start, then progress and app-specific messages (typically from execution loops), then end.
- No process runs more than one job at a time. An appServer may run many jobs over its life, one after another.
- A transient process IS its job.

THE CALLS, in spirit.core.jobs
- start(name), progress(done, total, text), end(result or error). Each is published, so the shell sees a job begin, move and finish.
- total 0 means unknown: the bar shows as indeterminate.
- A start while a job is open is refused by name. A server that gets more work while busy queues it itself.
- A transient process only calls progress: the node marks its start at spawn and its end at exit (complete/fail).

WHERE IT LIVES
- spirit.core.jobs (kernel.js) holds what every spawned process shares: report, log, complete, fail, publish, start, progress, end.
- publish moves out of appServer.js into spirit.core.jobs, size check with it; appServer.js keeps only what serving needs.
- appProcess.js is made only when something is unique to transient processes; nothing is yet.

THE SHELL
- One shared bar element draws a process's open job; a server between jobs shows idle, no bar.

chat.text:
G29.14 box is capped. Here is a shape for progress.
Every spawned job, server or transient, already reports through spirit.core.jobs.report in kernel.js; appServer.publish(obj) is a wrapper that sends {app: obj}. So one published object can serve both kinds.
Shape: {progress: {done, total, text}}. done and total are numbers, total 0 means unknown (an indeterminate bar), text is one short line.
Transient processes get spirit.core.jobs.progress(done, total, text) beside log/complete/fail; servers call appServer.publish({progress: ...}).
The bar is one shared shell element that reads the newest progress object of a job. Does that shape suit you?

Do we already have a standard process object like jst/appServer.js something like js/appProcess.js that provides transient processes with the node's startup loopback-port and the functions that appServers get?

No js/appProcess.js. A transient process gets spirit.core.jobs from kernel.js: report, log, complete, fail.
The node hands it SPIRIT_JOB_ID and SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL (the loopback door, port included); report() is the only place either is read.
appServer.js exports spirit, serve, publish, matches. Its publish is only report({app: obj}) with the size check, so a transient process could call it today without serving anything.
So a progress call can live in one place both kinds already load: kernel.js spirit.core.jobs, or a new appProcess.js. Which do you want?

spirit.core.jobs should contain the common stuff, appServer and, if neccessary, appProcess would only contain stuff unique to those two process types....

how is this organized now?

Now: spirit.core.jobs (kernel.js) holds the common part, report, log, complete and fail, which every spawned process can call.
appServer.js holds the server-only part (serve, the verb checks, its own error codes, dependencies, agents rules, debug), plus publish. publish is common by your rule: it is only report({app}) with the size check.
There is no appProcess.js; the transient ones (wordpressScanner, imageStats, imageCaptionClaude and Batch) call spirit.core.jobs.log/complete/fail directly.
